title: Comparing a value to True/False with == instead of using its truthiness
purpose: Prevent the idiom 'if x == True / == False' an authoring LLM emits from memorised snippets, which misbehaves when x's __eq__ or __bool__ is unusual and reads as if x must already be a bool.
trigger: A boolean condition literally compares an expression to the constants True or False with ==/!= without having first forced it to a bool (for example 'x == True' in an if/while).
correct: Use the value's own truthiness: 'if x:' / 'if not x:', or coerce once with bool(x) when you genuinely need a strict bool, or test identity 'is True' only where the object is known to be exactly the singleton True.
compiler_relationship: Advisory rule: valid syntax, but == True is almost never the intended semantics and looks wrong to later reader.
return_semantics: A LanguageRulePage may be opened and then returned to the originating cycle.
